# Contributing

Thanks for considering contributing to Universal Locks! Please follow the guidelines below so the contribution process goes smoothly.

> This plugin uses [Carbonoxide](https://github.com/maxijonson/carbonoxide) for its tooling. If you like how it's set up, give it a try for your next Rust plugin!

## Do not edit the root `UniversalLocks.cs` file

The root `UniversalLocks.cs` file is generated by the build, so don't edit it directly. Make your changes in the source files under `src` instead. You can (and should) commit the root file after building, but anything you change in it by hand gets overwritten the next time the plugin is built. **If a change is made in the root file but not in the source files, it will be lost**.

## Setup

I develop this plugin with [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and the [C# Dev Kit](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-dotnettools.csdevkit) extension. You can use other IDEs, but I can't guarantee everything will work the same.

**Prerequisites**

- [dotnet](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/download/dotnet) SDK, for building the plugin and running the build scripts
- Windows, for running the Rust servers and the scripts
- [NodeJS](https://nodejs.org/) (optional), for [merging partial classes](#merging-partial-classes)

**Environments**

The plugin supports both Oxide and Carbon, so it gets tested on local Rust servers for both. I call each one an environment. An environment is a local Rust server for one framework (Oxide or Carbon) on one Steam branch, which gives 4 of them:

| Environment         | Framework | Rust branch | Port  |
| ------------------- | --------- | ----------- | ----- |
| `oxide-production`  | Oxide     | `public`    | 28015 |
| `oxide-staging`     | Oxide     | `staging`   | 28016 |
| `carbon-production` | Carbon    | `public`    | 28025 |
| `carbon-staging`    | Carbon    | `staging`   | 28026 |

Production is the `public` branch with the framework's stable build. It's what server owners are running right now. Staging is Rust's `staging` branch with the framework's staging build. It previews the next Rust update, not the next version of the plugin, so it's where you check that the plugin won't break when that update ships.

Each environment lives in its own folder under `servers` and they can all run at the same time. You don't need all 4 though. The build only targets the environments you have a server for, so if you don't care about staging, just skip the staging scripts.

**Create the servers**

1. Run `dotnet tool restore` to install [MJSU's Plugin.Merge](https://github.com/dassjosh/Plugin.Merge) and CSharpier.
2. (Optional) Run `npm install` to install the [partial classes merging](#merging-partial-classes) script's dependencies.
3. Run the `update_*.bat` scripts (not the `_update_*.bat` ones!) to create the servers in the `servers` folder. Each one is a full Rust server, around 8.5 GB. Run them again whenever Rust or the framework gets an update.
4. Run each `run_*.bat` script once so the framework sets itself up, then stop the server once it's done loading. On Oxide, this writes the publicized game assemblies to `servers/oxide-*/publicized`, which the build needs. Oxide only writes them when it compiles a plugin, so `_run.bat` puts a placeholder `CarbonoxidePublicize` plugin in the server until they exist. Do this again after every update so the build gets the latest assemblies.
5. In each Carbon server's `servers/carbon-*/carbon/config.json`, set `DeveloperMode` to `true`, then run the server again. Carbon then generates the developer assemblies the build needs.

Universal Locks doesn't depend on any other plugin. If you want to test it alongside other plugins, drop them in `dependencies/plugins` and run `copy_dependencies.bat`. Everything in `dependencies` gets copied into each server's `oxide` or `carbon` folder.

To join a server, use the F1 console with the environment's port:

```
client.connect localhost:28015
```

## Building the plugin

```bash
# Build against oxide-production, merge, format and copy to all servers
dotnet build plugin.csproj

# Same thing, but rebuilds whenever you save a file
dotnet watch build --project plugin.csproj

# Build for a specific environment (merge, format and copy to that server only)
dotnet build oxide-production.csproj
dotnet build oxide-staging.csproj
dotnet build carbon-production.csproj
dotnet build carbon-staging.csproj
```

`plugin.csproj` is the one I use while coding, but keep in mind it only compiles against oxide-production. Use `ValidateAll` to check the rest.

## Validating all environments

To check that the plugin compiles on every environment at once:

```bash
dotnet msbuild plugin.csproj -restore -t:ValidateAll
```

This runs the normal build first, then compiles `src` against each environment you have a server for, and compiles the merged `UniversalLocks.cs` the same way both an Oxide and a Carbon server would.

## VS Code setup

- Use the `Tasks: Run Build Task` command to see all the build tasks, instead of typing out the commands above.
- To switch between the Oxide and Carbon project contexts (e.g. to see code inside `#if CARBON` light up), use the `CSharp: Change the active document's project context` command while inside a `.cs` file and pick the environment's project.

## Merging partial classes

Plugin.Merge merges all the files in `src` into one, but at the time of writing, it just appends partial classes one after another as it finds them, which gets messy for anyone reading the merged plugin (curators included).

The [`post-merge.ts`](scripts/post-merge.ts) script merges them into a single class declaration. The build runs it automatically when it finds NodeJS and the `node_modules` folder, so `npm install` is all you need. Right now the only partial class is `UniversalLocks` itself, so without NodeJS the only difference is that the root class keeps its `partial` keyword. The build still works fine, but your `UniversalLocks.cs` won't match the committed one, so please set it up before opening a PR if you can.

## Conventions

The point of splitting the plugin into multiple files is to keep the code organized and easy to maintain. Please follow the existing file structure and conventions when adding new features or making changes.

> In general, I'm pretty loose about where files go, but I'll be strict when it comes to file size.
>
> Being a Web developer primarily, where I'm used to have everything contained into their own file (each components, services, functions, etc. have their own file), **I really hate** insanely large files.

- **Contained Responsibility**: Each file should have a clear and focused responsibility. Think about how the plugin may grow over time and build a structure that won't end up bloating a single file. Avoid mixing multiple functionalities in a single file. I would rather over-simplify now than refactor later.
  - For example: All hooks are in their own file under the `Hooks` folder, rather than having one `UniversalLocks.Hooks.cs` file that may grow over time. Even if some of them are less than 10 lines, the idea is that the plugin may grow and more hooks may be added in the future. Growing the number of files is preferred over growing the size of existing files.
- **Folder Structure**: Organize files in a way that makes sense and try to group related files together. You don't need to break your head over this though, there may be more than one acceptable place to add your file. Just make it easy to guess where they belong.
- **Root Plugin Class**: Keep root class (`UniversalLocks`) methods and fields in the `Plugin` folder. Always prefix files under the `Plugin` folder with `UniversalLocks.` to signal that they belong to the root class. The `Plugin` folder is basically a single large `UniversalLocks.cs` file split into multiple files.
- **Namespaces**: Use `UniversalLocksPlugin.` followed by the top-most parent folder name under `src`. For example, the file `src/Plugin/Hooks/UniversalLocks.Init.cs` uses the namespace `UniversalLocksPlugin.Plugin` because `Plugin` is the top-most parent folder relative to `src`.
- **Build Warnings & Errors**: Make sure your code compiles without any warnings or errors before opening a pull request. Nullable warnings are already treated as errors, and the other warnings should be treated the same way.

## Before Submitting a Pull Request

Before submitting a pull request, please make sure that:

- Your code follows the existing coding style and conventions used in the project.
- `dotnet msbuild plugin.csproj -restore -t:ValidateAll` passes with no warnings.
- You have tested your changes on both oxide-production and carbon-production to make sure they work as expected on both frameworks. If a Rust update is coming up, test on the staging environments too.
